questions.question: What is the hallmark histological feature of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)?
questions.explanation: The defining histological finding is activated macrophages engulfing erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets in bone marrow, spleen, liver or lymph node tissue. Note that it is neither sensitive nor specific — it may be absent early in the disease, so its absence does not exclude HLH and the diagnosis rests on the full clinical and biochemical picture. Cytopenias and organomegaly are common features of HLH but are clinical/laboratory findings, not the histological hallmark.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in the pathophysiology of HLH?
questions.explanation: HLH is a hyperinflammatory syndrome driven by a cytokine storm (IFN-gamma, IL-1, IL-6, IL-18, TNF-alpha, soluble IL-2 receptor) with massive macrophage activation — the opposite of suppressed macrophage activity. Impaired cytotoxic function of NK cells and CD8 T lymphocytes is the upstream defect that prevents clearance of the antigenic stimulus, so the option about ineffective T lymphocytes is a genuine near-miss; ESICM's answer key points to the downstream uncontrolled cytokine release as the characteristic finding.

questions.question: What is the primary trigger for HLH in the context of infection?
questions.explanation: Herpes group viruses are the commonest infectious trigger of secondary HLH, with EBV clearly dominant and associated with the worst outcomes. Visceral leishmaniasis, mycobacteria and SARS-CoV-2 are all recognised triggers and should be actively excluded — leishmaniasis in particular because it is treatable and mimics HLH — but they are far less frequent than the herpesviruses.

questions.question: Which diagnostic scoring system is considered a bedside probability tool for HLH?
questions.explanation: The HScore was derived and validated in adults with reactive haemophagocytic syndrome and gives a probability of HLH from nine weighted variables (known immunosuppression, temperature, organomegaly, cytopenias, ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, AST, haemophagocytosis on marrow), which makes it usable at the bedside. The HLH-2004 criteria were developed for paediatric familial HLH trials and require tests such as NK cell activity and soluble CD25 that are rarely available acutely, so they function as trial entry criteria rather than a bedside probability tool.

questions.question: Which therapy is considered a second-line option for HLH and is particularly associated with potential complications like PRES and secondary leukaemia?
questions.explanation: Etoposide is a topoisomerase II inhibitor that depletes activated T cells and macrophages; its recognised toxicities include posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, myelosuppression and treatment-related secondary acute leukaemia. Corticosteroids are first-line and lack this profile, while anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) is used as an alternative or adjunct and is not associated with secondary leukaemia.

questions.question: Which factor directly correlates with an elevated risk of mortality in HLH patients?
questions.explanation: Ferritin is both a diagnostic marker and a prognostic one: very high levels correlate with mortality, and failure of ferritin to fall with treatment predicts a poor outcome, which is why serial measurement is used to track response. Cytopenias, organomegaly and neurological involvement are diagnostic or clinical features of the syndrome rather than the variable ESICM identifies as directly correlating with mortality risk.

questions.question: You have been asked to cover the Haematology-Oncology Unit and have been asked by the nursing staff whether it is appropriate to request blood tests to monitor for tumour lysis syndrome for a new admission. Your patient is a 52-year-old woman who has been recently diagnosed with adult T cell leukaemia with bulky disease. She has just been started on steroids before planned chemotherapy tomorrow. She has a history of hypertension and is on amlodipine. Her pre-treatment bloodwork showed: Creatinine 95 µmol/l, Uric acid 450 µmol/l, LDH ≥ 2 x ULN. Which of the following would put her in a higher risk category for developing tumour lysis syndrome?
options: Adult T cell leukaemia with bulky disease
questions.explanation: Adult T cell leukaemia with bulky disease falls in the high-risk cancers category. Other patient specific risks include being male and aged >65 years old. Biochemical parameters indicating a higher risk of TLS include a pre-treatment serum uric acid level > 7.5 mg/dL (446.1 µmol/l) and creatinine >123.8 µmol/l.

questions.question: You have been asked to review a Haematology-Oncology patient admitted on to the High Dependency Unit for monitoring. The patient is a 73-year-old male who has just been started on Venetoclax today after being diagnosed with CLL recently. Imaging showed lymph nodes measuring ≥10cm and blood work shows an absolute lymphocyte count ≥ 25 x 109/l. Which of the following statements are True/False?

statements.label: A
statements.text: His risk of developing tumour lysis syndrome is low

statements.label: B
statements.text: Starting allopurinol, not rasburicase, is more appropriate in this scenario

statements.label: C
statements.text: Cautious intravenous hydration is recommended to prevent AKI while balancing risk of fluid overload

statements.label: D
statements.text: In cases where diuresis is required, thiazide diuretics are first line in terms of diuretics.

questions.explanation: A. FALSE: CLL with lymph nodes ≥10cm or lymph nodes ≥5cm and absolute lymphocyte count ≥ 25 x 109/l are considered high risk cancers. B. FALSE: Rasburicase is indicated in TLS prophylaxis of high-risk cancers, whereas allopurinol is indicated in low-risk cancers. C. TRUE. D. FALSE: In cases where diuresis is required e.g. fluid overload, loop diuretics are preferred as they promote diuresis and potentially enhance potassium secretion. Thiazide diuretics can elevate uric acid levels and should be avoided.
